label: calculus & precalculus batch — limits, derivatives, conics, polar, identities, function analysis

widget.prompt: Zoom in on x = 4 for f(x) = x² − 5. Watch both sides and the point itself before deciding.
widget.successFeedback: All three agree at 11: the left limit, the right limit and f(4). That triple agreement is exactly what 'continuous' means, and it is why direct substitution is legal here — not a shortcut, but the definition cashed out.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Zoom in at least twice more. A limit is about what happens arbitrarily close to 4, which one view cannot show.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: Look again at the two one-sided values. They agree, so the limit exists.

widget.prompt: As x grows, (3x² + 1)/(x² − 5) settles somewhere. Zoom to watch both sides converge on that level.
widget.successFeedback: It settles at 3 — the ratio of leading coefficients, 3/1. Equal degrees means the +1 and the −5 stop mattering as x grows; only the x² terms still count, and the horizontal asymptote is their ratio.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Zoom further. The settling only becomes obvious once the smaller terms are visibly irrelevant.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: Both sides approach the same level, so the limit exists.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x² + 1 at x = 2, check the three things continuity requires: the left limit, the right limit, and the value.
widget.successFeedback: All three read 5. Continuity at a point is a three-part test — f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they are EQUAL — and a function can fail any one of them independently, which is what the next lessons exploit.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Zoom in again to be sure the two sides really coincide rather than nearly coinciding.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: The one-sided values agree, so the limit exists.

widget.prompt: For (x² + 1)/(x − 3), zoom in on x = 3 and watch the two sides head in opposite directions.
widget.successFeedback: No limit: one side dives, the other climbs. A vertical asymptote is a two-sided disagreement, and it is why 'the limit is infinity' is a description of the failure rather than a value.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Keep zooming. The disagreement grows rather than settling, which is the whole point.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: The two sides do not approach a common value, so no limit exists here.

widget.prompt: Trace f(x) = x² until the tangent slope reads 6, then consider what 3f would do to that reading.
widget.successFeedback: Slope 6 at x = 3, since f′(x) = 2x. Multiplying the function by 3 multiplies every one of these slopes by 3 — the constant rides along untouched, which is the whole constant-multiple rule seen rather than stated.
widget.lowFeedback: The tangent is still shallower than 6.
widget.highFeedback: The tangent has passed a slope of 6.

widget.prompt: Trace f(x) = x³ until the tangent slope reads 12. Then ask what the slope of the SLOPE is doing.
widget.successFeedback: Slope 12 at x = 2, since f′(x) = 3x². The first derivative is how fast f changes; the second is how fast THAT changes — position, velocity, acceleration are the same three questions asked of one curve.
widget.lowFeedback: The tangent is still shallower than 12.
widget.highFeedback: The tangent has passed a slope of 12.

widget.prompt: Trace f(x) = x² until the tangent slope reads 4. The inverse curve's slope at the matching point is the reciprocal.
widget.successFeedback: Slope 4 at x = 2. Reflecting a curve across y = x swaps run and rise, so every slope becomes its own reciprocal — the inverse of x² has slope 1/4 at the matching point, and that is why the reciprocal rule needs no separate proof.
widget.lowFeedback: The tangent is still shallower than 4.
widget.highFeedback: The tangent has passed a slope of 4.

widget.prompt: Slide the eccentricity to 0.8 and watch the two foci separate from the centre.
widget.successFeedback: e = c/a = 0.8, so with a = 5 the focal distance c is 4 — and 4² = 5² − 3² confirms b = 3. The a-b-c relation is not a formula to memorise: it is the right triangle joining centre, focus and co-vertex.
widget.explorationFeedback: Move the slider a few more times. The relationship between the foci and the shape only shows up across a range, not at one setting.
widget.lowFeedback: Eccentricity still below 0.8 — the ellipse is rounder than the target.
widget.highFeedback: Eccentricity above 0.8 — the ellipse is flatter than the target.

widget.prompt: Slide the eccentricity to 0.6 and watch the two focal distances as the point travels — their SUM is what to keep an eye on.
widget.successFeedback: The two distances trade off but always total the same 2a. That constant sum is the ellipse's definition — the pin-and-string construction — and the eccentricity only decides how far apart the pins sit.
widget.explorationFeedback: Slide a few more times. The claim is that the sum is constant for EVERY position, which one snapshot cannot establish.

widget.prompt: Push the eccentricity past 1 — to 1.5 — and watch the closed curve break open.
widget.successFeedback: Past e = 1 the ellipse becomes a hyperbola. For x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 with a = 3 and c = 5, e = 5/3 ≈ 1.67 and the foci sit at (±5, 0) on the opening axis. Eccentricity is one dial running through every conic: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.
widget.explorationFeedback: Slide across e = 1 a few times to see the transition rather than just the endpoint.
widget.lowFeedback: Still below 1.5 — the curve has not opened as far as the target.

widget.prompt: Earth's orbit is nearly circular. Slide the eccentricity down to 0.2 and watch where the focus sits.
widget.successFeedback: At low eccentricity the ellipse is almost a circle, but the focus is still NOT the centre — and that is Kepler's first law: the Sun sits at a focus, not the middle. Earth's real eccentricity is 0.017, which is why the orbit looks circular while the seasons still differ in length.
widget.explorationFeedback: Slide across a range first; the focus-versus-centre distinction is easiest to see while the shape is changing.
widget.lowFeedback: Below 0.2 — even rounder than the target.

widget.prompt: Trace r = 3 cos(2θ) and count the petals that appear.
widget.successFeedback: Four petals from a coefficient of 2 — an even coefficient doubles into 2n petals, an odd one gives exactly n. Watching the trace makes the rule obvious: the curve retraces itself on the second lap only when n is odd.
widget.lowFeedback: Fewer petals than the target — raise the coefficient.
widget.highFeedback: More petals than the target — lower the coefficient.

widget.prompt: Trace a curve of radius 3 and watch how a polar address is built: a distance out, and an angle round.
widget.successFeedback: A polar point is (r, θ) — how far, then which way. (3, π/2) means three units out along the quarter-turn direction, which lands on the positive y-axis. The trace shows the angle sweeping while r stays fixed.

widget.prompt: Trace x² to x = −2 and read the height, then compare it with the height at x = +2.
widget.successFeedback: Both give 4. A function is EVEN when f(−x) = f(x) — the graph is its own mirror image across the vertical axis — and x⁴ − 3x² behaves the same way for the same reason: every exponent is even.
widget.lowFeedback: Still to the right of x = −2.

widget.prompt: Trace x² to x = 3 and read the height, then find the other input that reaches the same height.
widget.successFeedback: Height 9 at x = 3, and also at x = −3. Two inputs sharing one output is exactly what the horizontal line test detects, and it is why x² has no inverse until the domain is cut in half.

widget.prompt: Widen the secant to span 6 units and read its slope — the average rate of change over that whole interval.
widget.successFeedback: Average rate = rise over run, and the units come with it: a tank going from 48 to 12 gallons over 6 minutes changes at (12 − 48)/6 = −6 gallons per minute. The sign says draining, and the unit says what is being counted per what.
widget.lowFeedback: The interval is still narrower than 6.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 1), zoom in on x = 1 and decide what kind of break this is.
widget.successFeedback: A vertical asymptote at x = 1: the denominator vanishes but the numerator does not, so the two sides fly apart. Compare that with x = 2, where BOTH vanish and the break is a removable hole instead — same-looking equation, different behaviour.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Zoom further. The sides separate more as you go, which is what distinguishes an asymptote from a hole.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: The two sides disagree without bound, so no limit exists.

widget.prompt: f(x) = (x² + 3x + 5)/(x + 1) has no horizontal asymptote. Zoom out along the curve and watch it settle onto a straight line instead.
widget.successFeedback: It hugs a slanted line, not a level one. When the numerator's degree is exactly one more than the denominator's, the curve approaches a SLANT asymptote — division gives x + 2 plus a remainder that fades away.
widget.moreZoomFeedback: Keep going. The straight-line behaviour only emerges once the remainder becomes negligible.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: The curve approaches a definite line here.

refusals.title: Shifted conics, second-degree form, completing the square, asymptote equations
refusals.why: conicLocusLab's only manipulable is eccentricity in tenths — it models the SHAPE family, not a translated centre, an A/C-coefficient classification, or the algebra of completing the square on two variables at once. quadraticExplore handles a single-variable vertex form and cannot represent x²/25 + y²/9 = 1. Refused.

refusals.title: Polar↔rectangular conversion, nth roots, parametric motion
refusals.why: polarTrace draws rose and limacon curves; it has no coordinate-conversion state, no root-of-unity display, and no time parameter. Parametric projectile work needs a t-slider driving two coordinates independently and no engine offers one. This is an engine gap, not a fit failure: a `parametricMotionLab` would convert five of these seven. Refused pending that decision.

refusals.lesson: polynomial-rational-analysis/pra-01-01, pra-01-03, pra-02-01, pra-02-02, pra-02-03, pra-05-01
refusals.title: Rational root theorem, synthetic division, FTA, conjugate pairs, sign charts
refusals.why: These are symbolic-procedure lessons — list divisor candidates, run synthetic division, count zeros with multiplicity, build a quadratic from a conjugate pair. graphZoom models limit behaviour at a point; quadraticExplore models a vertex. Nothing represents a division tableau or a candidate list as manipulable state. Refused.

refusals.title: Rationalizing, the IVT, series partial sums
refusals.why: lc-02-03 is a symbolic conjugate-multiplication step; lc-04-03 asks what the IVT guarantees, a statement about a theorem rather than a quantity; lc-05-03 sums a geometric series. graphZoom shows behaviour AT a point and has no series accumulator. sequenceBuild dials a common ratio but does not accumulate partial sums. Refused.

refusals.title: Quotient rule, choosing rules, chains within chains, implicit differentiation
refusals.why: derivativeTrace traces ONE named curve (square | cubic | abs) and reads its slope. It cannot represent a quotient of two arbitrary functions, a nested composition, or an implicitly defined circle. These need a symbolic differentiation surface that does not exist. Refused.

refusals.lesson: function-analysis/fna-03-02, fna-03-03, fna-04-01, fna-04-02, fna-04-03, fna-05-02
refusals.title: Piecewise evaluation, composition, decomposition, domain restriction
refusals.why: Composition and decomposition manipulate function DEFINITIONS rather than values; derivativeTrace's fn enum is square|cubic|abs, so it cannot hold an arbitrary f and g. Piecewise evaluation selects a branch, which no engine exposes as state. Refused.

refusals.title: Cofunction, double-angle and negative-angle identities
refusals.why: BLOCKED BY STRUCTURE, NOT BY FIT — a third category. unitCircleExplore's ghost modes (cofunction | double | negate) are purpose-built for exactly these three lessons and the configs were written and math-verified. But each lesson's SOLE interactive step carries a `predict` block, and the applier correctly refuses to convert one: the predict prompt asks the learner to forecast the CURRENT widget's behaviour, so swapping the widget beneath it would leave the prediction asking about something that is no longer there. Converting these needs the predict prompt rewritten alongside the widget — authoring, not a swap. Recorded separately from fit refusals: the engine fits, the step is protected.
